title: Knots, rope and lifting
summary: Nine essential knots with what each is for, how to tie it and where it fails, plus rope and strap working loads, pulley and lever gain, and safe handling of heavy salvage. Everything is set to conservative safety factors from published rope, cargo and rigging sources.

steps.text: Pick the knot from the table by what you need: a loop, a hitch to a post, an adjustable line, or a joint between two ropes. Practise it until you can tie it without looking.
Work out the load. Divide the breaking strength by 5 (by 10 for climbing lines, and by 15 for rescue or anything lifting a person) to get the working load.
steps.warn: Knots, wear, sun and shock loads cut strength. A knotted rope can lose up to half.

steps.text: Plan the lift: use help, levers or pulleys, and cribbing under anything raised.
Stay out from under suspended or jacked loads. Get a rigger for overhead work.
steps.warn: A jack alone is never safe support. Put stands or cribbing under the load before anyone goes beneath it.

notes:
## Before you start
Every knot weakens rope. Rope, strap and chain have a **working load limit (WLL)** far below **breaking strength**. Stay under the WLL and never stand under a load.

## Essential knots
| Knot | Use it for | Tie it (short) | Limits |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Bowline** | Fixed loop at a rope end, or tying a rope to an anchor (US Army) | Make a loop in the standing part. Pull a bight of the standing part up through it. Pass the end through the bight and back on itself. Dress it, add an overhand safety (US Army) | Must be dressed and set. Secure the tail if it matters (USFS). Can work loose when slack (Frostburg) |
| **Clove hitch** | Temporary tie to a post, pole or tree (US Navy, USFS) | Two turns round the anchor, crossing over the standing part, end tucked under the cross. Add two half hitches (US Army) | Not for life support (USFS). Can work itself out if slack (US Navy) |
| **Two half hitches** (round turn first) | Tying a rope end to a ring, post or spar (US Army) | One full turn round the anchor, then two half hitches over the standing part. Leave a tail of at least 10 cm (4 in) (US Army) | Needs constant tension (US Army) |
| **Taut-line hitch** | Adjustable loop for tent guylines and tarps (NRS) | End round the anchor, twice round the standing part inside the loop, one half hitch outside it. Dress (NRS) | Slides when slack, jams under load. No load rating given (NRS) |
| **Trucker's hitch** | Tightening a ridgeline or tie-down (Knots Manual) | Figure-eight loop near the end. End round the anchor and back through the loop. Pull. Finish with two half hitches (Knots Manual) | 3:1 on paper, about 2:1 in practice. Half hitches can jam after heavy or shock loads (Knots Manual) |
| **Sheet bend** | Joining two ropes (Frostburg). A becket bend suits ropes of different size (US Navy) | Same pattern as a bowline, with a bight in one rope as the loop (Frostburg) | Can loosen when slack. A double sheet bend is more secure (Frostburg) |
| **Figure-eight loop** | Fixed loop in a rope (US Army) | Make a 30 cm (12 in) bight. Turn it 360 degrees round the standing part. Pass the bight through the loop. Dress, no twists (US Army) | Keeps about 75-80 % of rope strength (Frostburg) |
| **Reef (square) knot** | Joining two ropes of equal diameter (US Army, US Navy) | Right over left, then left over right. Dress. Add an overhand on each side (US Army) | Each end must lie beside its own standing part, or it is a slipping granny (US Navy) or a "killer square" that falls apart (Frostburg). Can jam (US Navy). Keeps only 43-47 % of strength (Frostburg) |
| **Prusik** | Friction hitch: grips when loaded, slides when free (USFS) | Lay a cord loop on the rope. Pass the loop end round the rope and back through itself (CMC), making two turns with a locking bar across them (US Army). Dress, set, test under load (USFS) | Cord no thicker than the rope. Thinner, softer cord grips harder. Stiffer cord slides easier (USFS) |

## Working load and breaking strength
**WLL = minimum breaking strength / safety factor** (Samson). Use a higher factor for shock loads, sustained loads and anything involving people (Samson).

| Item | Rule |
|---|---|
| Rope, general use | Safety factor 5:1, so WLL is about 20 % of breaking strength (Samson, USFS) |
| Climbing or life-support rope | 10:1, about 10 % (Samson). Rescue rope and anything lifting a person: 15:1, about 7 % (NFPA 1983, USFS). USFS uses about 7 % |
| Knots in rope | Can cost up to 50 % of strength. A splice keeps about 100 % (Samson) |
| Web or ratchet strap | Design factor 3:1, so WLL is one-third of breaking strength (RAC). The weakest part sets the WLL (FMCSA) |


Default WLL when a US tie-down is unmarked (FMCSA); a marked value always wins:

| Material | WLL |
|---|---|
| Webbing 50 mm (2 in) | 910 kg (2,000 lb) |
| Nylon rope 13 mm (1/2 in) | 240 kg (525 lb) |
| Chain 10 mm (3/8 in), Grade 80 | 3,200 kg (7,100 lb) |

Unmarked welded chain counts as Grade 30, the weakest. Total WLL of the ties on a load must be at least half its weight (FMCSA).

## Pulleys and levers
| System | Ideal gain | Real life |
|---|---|---|
| Moving pulley on the load | 2:1 (CMC) | Less, because of friction (CMC) |
| 3:1 "Z" rig | 1 kN pull lifts 3 kN (CMC) | 2.57:1 with 85 % pulleys, 2.85:1 with 95 % (CMC) |

- A pulley fixed to the anchor only changes direction. A pulley on the load adds gain (CMC).
- More gain means more rope to pull: a simple 5:1 needs 5 m of rope pulled per 1 m of lift (CMC).
- A carabiner used as a pulley is about 50 % efficient (CMC).
- A lever's gain is the ratio of its arm lengths, and the work done is unchanged (UCSB).

## Lifting heavy salvage
- Test the weight first. Use two people, or a hoist, dolly or wheelbarrow (CCOHS).
- Keep the load close to your body, between shoulder and knee height. Step, do not twist (CCOHS).
- Jacks lift, stands hold. Once lifted, support the load on jack stands or cribbing before anyone works under it (Virginia DMME).
- Build cribs on firm, level ground from solid hardwood timbers, never round, triangular or smooth objects. Plan a safety factor of at least 4 (Virginia DMME).
- Chock the wheels. Lift only at the maker's lift points (Virginia DMME).
- Keep everyone clear of a suspended load. Never pull a sling out from under a resting load. Never shorten a sling with knots (OSHA).

## Ratchet straps and chain
- Read the WLL tag. Never knot, splice or repair webbing (RAC).
- Retire a strap with cuts, holes, worn stitching, UV damage, melting, chemical burns or knots (RAC).
- Put at least 6 in (15 cm) of webbing through the spool slot and take two full turns. Make sure the pawl is fully engaged. Do not extend the handle or winch bar with a pipe (RAC).
- For overhead lifting use only Grade 80 or 100 alloy chain (Crosby). Cut the WLL by 20 % for a choke hitch. Hooks must carry the load, never the latch (Crosby).

**Get a rigger or crane operator** for anything overhead, over people, or too heavy for a team.
